options.text: The number of containers involved — Compose is meant for a handful, while an orchestrator is required once a dozen or more are running.
options.why: Compose has no such container-count limit; a dozen containers on one host is well within its normal use, and container count is not what makes something an orchestrator.

options.text: Whether the containers are described declaratively — Compose is imperative, while an orchestrator always requires declarative YAML.
options.why: A Compose file is itself declarative, describing services, networks and volumes to be created; declarativeness is not what separates it from an orchestrator.

options.text: Whether the containers were built from a Dockerfile — Compose only runs pre-built images, while an orchestrator can build them too.
options.why: A Compose file can reference a build context the same way a plain `docker build` can; build capability is not the dividing line described here.

items.rationale: Compose and an orchestrator are a named confusable pair, and the dividing line is hosts plus persistence of intent: Compose applies a file to one machine once, while an orchestrator schedules across a fleet and keeps reconciling afterward — not how many containers are involved.

items.stem: A project's Compose file defines a web service, a worker service, and a shared database, and `docker compose up -d` is run. What creates, and in what relationship?

options.text: It creates the network, volumes, and containers for all three services on the single host where the command ran, in dependency order, and detaches immediately.
options.why: `-d` runs it detached; Compose brings up every declared service together on that one machine, respecting the dependencies declared between them.

options.text: It distributes the three services across whichever machines in the local network have spare capacity, balancing the load automatically.
options.why: Compose is a single-host tool; every service in the project runs on the one machine where the command was issued, with no cross-host distribution.

options.text: It only creates the containers, leaving the operator to run `docker volume` and `docker run -v` manually for anything the file declares, treating `up` as a containers-only subset of what the file describes.
options.why: Compose creates the network and volumes declared in the file as part of the same command, not as a separate manual step.

options.text: It builds fresh images for all three services from their Dockerfiles every time, regardless of whether anything changed.
options.why: `docker compose up` reuses existing images unless a rebuild is requested with `--build`; it does not rebuild unconditionally on every invocation.

items.rationale: `docker compose up` creates the network, volumes, and containers declared in the file, in dependency order, all on the single host the command runs on; `-d` detaches so the shell returns immediately while the services keep running.

items.stem: A machine running a Compose project loses power overnight. What happens to the application when it comes back, if no one intervenes?

options.text: It stays down, because Compose has no cross-host scheduling or automatic rescheduling after a host failure — nothing was watching to bring it back.
options.why: Compose applies the file once when the command is run; once that machine is gone, nothing external notices or reacts on its own.

options.text: It resumes automatically on the same machine, since Compose registers a restart policy with the host's boot process by default.
options.why: Compose configures no such automatic boot-time recovery by default; nothing restarts the project unless the operator runs the command again.

options.text: It migrates to another machine on the network automatically, since Compose treats every project as a pool of interchangeable hosts That framing credits Compose with cluster-wide scheduling, a capability it was never built to provide.
options.why: Compose has no concept of a pool of hosts at all; it is bound to the single machine where the command was run.

options.text: It resumes only the database service, since Compose prioritizes services declared with persistent volumes over stateless ones.
options.why: Compose applies no such prioritization on its own; without the command being run again, nothing in the project restarts regardless of which services declare volumes.

items.rationale: Compose has no cross-host scheduling and no rescheduling after a host failure: if the machine dies, the application dies with it, and nothing brings it back until the command is run again — the exact gap an orchestrator is built to close.

items.stem: An operator stops a Compose project with `docker compose stop` instead of bringing it down, then wonders why the network and containers are still visible in `docker ps -a`. What is the distinction?

options.text: Stopping halts the containers without removing them or the network; only bringing the project down deletes the containers and network it created.
options.why: Stop and down are different operations, mirroring the container-level distinction between stopping and removing.

options.text: There is no distinction, and both commands are expected to remove the containers and network identically.
options.why: Stopping a project merely halts it; only bringing it down removes the containers and network, so the two commands are not interchangeable.

options.text: The visibility in `docker ps -a` is a stale cache and will clear itself automatically within a few minutes regardless of which command was used.
options.why: The containers genuinely still exist after a stop; this is not a caching artifact but the expected state of a stopped, unremoved container.

options.text: Stopping only affects services that declare a database volume, leaving stateless services running as before.
options.why: Stopping a project halts every service it declares, regardless of whether that service is stateless or stateful.

items.rationale: Stopping a Compose project halts its containers, mirroring `docker stop`; bringing it down removes the containers and network it created, mirroring `docker rm`. The two are not interchangeable, exactly as at the single-container level.

items.stem: A developer argues that running an application as root inside a container is harmless "because it is only a container." Why is that the wrong instinct?

options.text: Because the kernel is shared with the host, the isolation boundary a compromised root process must cross is thinner than a hypervisor's, so the consequences reach further than in a VM.
options.why: Shared-kernel isolation is weaker than a hypervisor boundary, which is exactly why root privileges inside a container carry more real risk than the phrase suggests.

options.text: It is not wrong, since container namespaces make root inside a container fully equivalent to an unprivileged user on the host, treating namespace isolation as a complete substitute for a hypervisor's boundary.
options.why: Namespaces narrow what a process can see, but they do not eliminate the shared-kernel attack surface a root process can still reach.

options.text: Because a registry automatically rejects any image that was built and run as root, making the practice self-correcting.
options.why: A registry stores whatever it is pushed and performs no inspection of which user an image runs as.

options.text: Because running as root disables the image's declared `EXPOSE` ports, leaving the application unreachable.
options.why: The user a process runs as has no effect on port publishing; `EXPOSE` and `-p` are unrelated to the container's user.

items.rationale: Container isolation is weaker than a virtual machine's because the kernel is shared, so a compromise inside a container that runs as root reaches further than the same compromise would inside a VM — the practical answer is running as a non-root user, not adding a scanner at the end.

items.stem: A registry credential is passed into a build with `ARG`, and a later Dockerfile instruction unsets the variable before the image is finished. Is the credential safe once the build completes?

options.text: No, it is still present in the layer where it was written, and unsetting it later does not erase it — it must never enter a layer in the first place.
options.why: A layer records history rather than current state, so a value written and then unset is still readable from the earlier layer that recorded it.

options.text: Yes, because unsetting a build argument removes it from every layer of the image, not just the one where the final value is read That framing treats a later layer as able to erase what an earlier layer already recorded, which layered images cannot do.
options.why: Layers are additive history; unsetting a variable in a later instruction changes the final metadata but does not retroactively remove it from the earlier layer.

options.text: Yes, but only if the base image was pinned to a specific version rather than left unpinned.
options.why: Pinning the base image's version affects reproducibility of the build, not whether an `ARG` value persists in a layer once written.

options.text: It depends on whether the credential was also set with `ENV` in addition to `ARG`, since only `ENV` values persist in layers.
options.why: Both an `ARG` value used during the build and an `ENV` default persist in the image's layers or configuration; using `ARG` alone does not make it safe.

items.rationale: A value passed through `ARG` or set with `ENV` persists in the image and can be recovered from it even if a later instruction unsets it, because layers record history and nothing erases an earlier one — the only reliable approach is to never write a secret into a layer at all.

items.stem: A team believes a one-time vulnerability scan performed when an image was first built is sufficient going forward. What is missing from that plan?

options.text: Scanning needs to be continuous, because vulnerabilities are discovered later in images that have not themselves changed at all.
options.why: A scan reflects known vulnerabilities at the moment it runs; new ones are disclosed over time against unchanged software, so a single scan goes stale.

options.text: Nothing is missing, since a base image that passed a scan once can never later be found vulnerable without the image itself changing.
options.why: New vulnerabilities are regularly disclosed in already-published software, so an unchanged image can become newly flagged with no rebuild involved.

options.text: The scan should have been run against the Dockerfile's text instead of the built image, since vulnerabilities live in instructions, not artifacts.
options.why: Vulnerabilities are found in the software packages inside the built image, not in the Dockerfile text describing how it was assembled.

options.text: The scan needs to be run once per container created from the image rather than once per image, since each container has its own writable layer.
options.why: Vulnerabilities live in the shared image layers, not in any single container's writable layer, so scanning per-container adds nothing a single image-level scan does not already cover.

items.rationale: Scanning is a continuous activity rather than a one-off, because vulnerabilities are discovered in images that have not changed at all — a smaller, version-pinned base image reduces what there is to find, but does not remove the need to keep checking.

items.stem: A production fleet needs to survive a node failure, scale up under load, and roll out new versions without downtime. A single-host Compose setup already runs the containers involved. What is missing, and why does adding more containers to the same host not fix it?

options.text: Orchestration across a pool of hosts with continuous reconciliation — the requirement is about surviving a host failure and rescheduling, which a bigger single host cannot provide.
options.why: The discriminating property is many hosts plus a controller that keeps comparing actual state to desired state, not how many containers run on one machine.

options.text: More containers on the same host, since orchestration is fundamentally about running a larger number of containers than Compose is designed for, rather than about surviving the loss of a host entirely.
options.why: Container count is not the discriminator; the requirement is surviving a host failure, which no number of containers on one host can satisfy.

options.text: A bigger base image with more resources allocated per container, so each one can absorb more load individually.
options.why: Resource allocation per container does not address a host dying entirely, which removes every container on it regardless of how well-resourced each one was.

options.text: A faster registry, so that images pull more quickly whenever the single host needs to restart a container.
options.why: Pull speed does not create the additional hosts, scheduling, or health-checking that surviving a node failure and scaling under load require.

items.rationale: The exam's alternative answer to an orchestration requirement is always a single-host tool, usually Compose. The discriminating property is multiple hosts plus continuous reconciliation — something that keeps comparing running state against declared state and acts on the difference indefinitely, which a single, larger host still cannot provide.

items.stem: A node running several workloads stops reporting heartbeats to the orchestrator. What happens to the workloads that were running on it?

options.text: They are recreated elsewhere, because nodes are watched the same way workloads are, and a node that stops reporting has its workloads rescheduled rather than left stranded.
options.why: Continuous reconciliation applies to node health too, not only to individual workload health, so a lost node's work is moved rather than abandoned.

options.text: They stay assigned to that node indefinitely, since an orchestrator only reacts to a workload crashing, never to a node going silent That framing narrows the orchestrator's health checks to process crashes only, ignoring node-level liveness monitoring entirely.
options.why: Nodes are health-checked the same way workloads are; a node that stops reporting triggers rescheduling of its workloads onto healthy nodes.

options.text: They are paused rather than recreated, waiting for a human operator to manually confirm the node is actually down.
options.why: Reconciliation acts automatically once a node is detected as unhealthy; it does not wait on a manual confirmation step before rescheduling.

options.text: They are removed permanently, since an orchestrator treats a lost node as a signal to reduce the declared replica count.
options.why: A lost node does not change what was declared; the orchestrator still works to satisfy the same declared count by scheduling replacements elsewhere.

items.rationale: Nodes are watched the same way individual instances are: a node that stops reporting has its workloads recreated elsewhere instead of left stranded, which is exactly the self-healing property a single-host tool cannot offer.

items.stem: A CI pipeline builds an image, pushes it, and submits an updated declaration to the cluster. Weeks later, a pod crashes and is replaced automatically. Which component is responsible for that replacement?

options.text: The orchestrator, because what keeps the declaration true afterward is the orchestrator's continuous reconciliation, not the pipeline that ran once at deploy time.
options.why: A pipeline runs and finishes; the orchestrator is what keeps comparing actual state to desired state indefinitely, long after the pipeline has stopped running.

options.text: The CI pipeline, since it is triggered automatically to rerun whenever any workload in the cluster crashes.
options.why: A pipeline builds and pushes; it plays no role in detecting a crashed workload weeks after it last ran and has no ongoing connection to the cluster's runtime state.

options.text: The registry, because it revalidates every pulled image on a fixed schedule and triggers a replacement when a pull fails That framing gives the registry an active monitoring role over already-running workloads that it does not have.
options.why: A registry only stores and serves images on request; it has no scheduling role and does not trigger replacements for crashed workloads.

options.text: The container runtime on the node, acting entirely on its own without any coordination from a cluster-level component.
options.why: The runtime on a node executes what it is told, but deciding to recreate a crashed workload and where to place it is the orchestrator's reconciliation logic, not an independent runtime decision.

items.rationale: Orchestration is not CI/CD: a pipeline builds the image, pushes it, and may submit the updated declaration, but what keeps that declaration true for the weeks afterward — including replacing a crashed workload — is the orchestrator, continuously reconciling.

items.stem: Someone claims the orchestrator itself is what starts container processes and isolates them, the same way a runtime does. What is wrong with that claim?

options.text: Orchestration is not a runtime: the orchestrator decides what should run where, while the runtime on each node is what actually starts and isolates the container.
options.why: Deciding placement and starting a process are different layers of responsibility, and collapsing them is exactly the confusion this concept warns against.

options.text: Nothing is wrong with it, since the orchestrator and the runtime are simply two names for the same underlying component.
options.why: They are distinct layers with distinct jobs — scheduling and reconciliation versus actually creating and isolating the process — not two names for one thing.

options.text: It is wrong only because orchestration also does not build or push images, which is a separate and unrelated gap in the claim.
options.why: That is a true additional gap, but it does not address the specific runtime-versus-orchestrator confusion the claim actually makes.

options.text: It is wrong only because orchestration operates on pods rather than containers, which is a Kubernetes-specific vocabulary issue That framing treats the mismatch as naming only, when the runtime and orchestrator genuinely perform different jobs.
options.why: That distinction is real but separate; the claim's core error is conflating the orchestrator's scheduling role with the runtime's execution role.

items.rationale: Orchestration is not a runtime and not containerization: the orchestrator decides what should run where, and the runtime on each node actually starts it, isolated with namespaces and cgroups, from an image that already exists.

items.stem: A statement describes Kubernetes as "governed by the CNCF, which also hosts it." Is that the correct relationship?

options.text: No, the CNCF hosts Kubernetes as a graduated project, but governance rests with Kubernetes' own Steering Committee, an elected body its charter names as the project's governing authority.
options.why: Hosting and governing are separated deliberately: the CNCF provides funding, infrastructure, and marketing support, while technical and community direction stays with the project's own structures.

options.text: Yes, since a graduated CNCF project is by definition directly governed by the foundation that hosts it.
options.why: Graduation describes hosting maturity, not governance; Kubernetes' own Steering Committee, not the CNCF, is named as its governing body.

options.text: No, because Kubernetes is not hosted by the CNCF at all, but by the Linux Foundation directly instead.
options.why: The CNCF, itself part of the Linux Foundation, is specifically the body that hosts Kubernetes as a graduated project.

options.text: Yes, and the Steering Committee referenced elsewhere is simply an internal CNCF department with no independent authority, treating hosting and governance as the same relationship rather than two deliberately separated ones.
options.why: The Steering Committee is Kubernetes' own elected governing body, distinct from and not subordinate to the CNCF's internal structure.

items.rationale: Two facts about Kubernetes' standing are routinely confused and both are examinable: it is hosted by the CNCF as a graduated project, and it is governed by its own Steering Committee — the CNCF hosts, funds, and supports; it does not govern.

items.stem: A candidate preparing for LFCA wonders whether they need to be able to write Kubernetes manifests and pass operational tasks like a CKA candidate. What level of Kubernetes knowledge does the exam actually expect?

options.text: Vocabulary and purpose — recognising what Kubernetes is for and naming its core objects — not operational skill such as writing manifests.
options.why: LFCA depth stays at recognition and understanding, deliberately stopping short of the hands-on skill a CKA-level assessment would require.

options.text: Full manifest-writing ability, since LFCA and CKA test the exact same depth of Kubernetes operational skill.
options.why: LFCA and CKA target different depths; LFCA stops at recognition and purpose, while CKA-level operational skill is explicitly out of scope here.

options.text: No Kubernetes knowledge at all, since the exam confines itself entirely to single-host Docker concepts.
options.why: Kubernetes vocabulary — cluster, node, control plane, pod, Deployment, Service — is explicitly part of the working vocabulary this exam expects.

options.text: Only enough to describe the CNCF's governance structure, with no expectation of naming any Kubernetes object That framing narrows the exam's scope to organisational trivia rather than the vocabulary and purpose it is actually built around.
options.why: Governance is one examinable fact among several; the exam also expects the working vocabulary of cluster, node, pod, Deployment, and Service.

items.rationale: LFCA wants vocabulary and purpose, not operational skill — recognising what Kubernetes is for and what its objects are called, not writing manifests or passing a CKA-level practical assessment.

items.stem: Someone draws an analogy between the CNCF's relationship to Kubernetes and the Linux Foundation's relationship to the Linux kernel. Is that comparison sound?

options.text: Yes, both foundations host and fund the project without setting its technical direction, which stays with the project's own governance structures.
options.why: The exam deliberately mirrors this shape across two different domains, and recognising the pattern is part of what makes the governance distinction memorable.

options.text: No, because the Linux Foundation directly sets the kernel's technical direction while the CNCF does not do the same for Kubernetes.
options.why: Neither foundation sets its hosted project's technical direction; both relationships are hosting and funding without governing.

options.text: No, because the CNCF is an entirely separate organisation from the Linux Foundation with no structural relationship between them.
options.why: The CNCF is part of the nonprofit Linux Foundation, not a separate, unrelated organisation.

options.text: Yes, but only because both projects share the exact same Steering Committee membership across kernel and Kubernetes decisions.
options.why: Kubernetes' Steering Committee and the Linux kernel's own governance are separate bodies for separate projects; the analogy is about structural shape, not shared membership.

items.rationale: The governance point mirrors a distinction the exam makes elsewhere: the Linux Foundation hosts and funds the Linux kernel without setting its technical direction, and the CNCF stands in the same relation to Kubernetes.

items.stem: A candidate is asked to place cluster, node, pod, and container in a containment hierarchy from largest to smallest. What is the correct order?

options.text: A cluster contains nodes, a node runs pods, and a pod holds containers.
options.why: Each layer contains the next: the cluster is the whole pool of machines, a node is one machine, and a pod is the unit of containers running on it.

options.text: A node contains clusters, a cluster runs pods, and a pod holds containers.
options.why: This reverses the cluster and the node; a cluster is the larger pool that a node belongs to, not the other way around.

options.text: A cluster contains pods directly, and nodes are an optional layer that some clusters omit entirely.
options.why: Every cluster needs at least one worker node in order to run pods at all; a node is not an optional layer.

options.text: A pod contains nodes, and a node runs directly inside a container.
options.why: This inverts the entire hierarchy; a node is a machine that runs pods, not something contained inside one.

items.rationale: Node, pod, and container form a containment hierarchy the exam expects a candidate to keep straight: a cluster contains nodes, a node runs pods, and a pod holds containers.

items.stem: A new pod remains stuck in a not-starting state, and every node in the cluster is already running workloads near its resource limit. What level does this problem resolve to?

options.text: The node level — no node has enough spare resource capacity for the scheduler to place the pod, which is exactly the constraint it schedules against.
options.why: The scheduler places workloads against node capacity, so "why is this pod not starting" frequently resolves to insufficient room on the available nodes.

options.text: The registry level, since a pod that cannot start is always evidence the image it references failed to be pulled.
options.why: The scenario describes nodes already at their resource limit, not a failed pull; a registry problem would surface differently.

options.text: The container level, since the pod's individual containers must each be resized before the pod as a whole can be scheduled That framing moves the scheduling decision down to individual containers, when the scheduler only ever places whole pods.
options.why: Scheduling decides which node a pod goes to as a whole; resizing individual containers inside it does not address the described lack of node capacity.

options.text: The Service level, since a stable network endpoint must exist before the scheduler will place any pod behind it.
options.why: A Service governs addressing after pods exist; it is not a prerequisite the scheduler checks before placing a pod on a node.

items.rationale: Node capacity is what the scheduler places workloads against, so a pod stuck not starting frequently resolves to a node-level answer — insufficient resources, or no node matching the pod's constraints.

items.stem: A node is drained for maintenance while it holds several running pods. What happens to those pods, and why is this considered safe?

options.text: They are recreated on other nodes, which is safe only because pods are treated as disposable and their replacements can serve requests just as well.
options.why: Draining relies on pod disposability; a replacement pod on another node is expected to be functionally equivalent to the one it replaces.

options.text: They pause in place on the draining node until it returns from maintenance, since draining never actually moves running pods That framing describes drain as inert, when its entire purpose is to evict and reschedule the pods running on that node.
options.why: Draining specifically causes a node's pods to be recreated elsewhere so maintenance can proceed without leaving workloads stranded on it.

options.text: They are deleted permanently, since draining is treated identically to scaling the replica count down to zero.
options.why: Draining moves workloads to other nodes rather than reducing any declared count; the pods are recreated, not permanently removed.

options.text: They are converted into a Service so that traffic can continue reaching the maintenance node directly.
options.why: A Service is an addressing abstraction in front of pods; draining a node has no effect that converts a pod into one.

items.rationale: Nodes are replaceable: draining one causes its pods to be recreated elsewhere, which is only safe because pods are treated as disposable rather than as irreplaceable, hand-tended processes.

items.stem: A scaling request asks for "five instances" of a service. One engineer interprets this as five pods; another as five containers inside one pod. Which is the Kubernetes model, and why does it matter?

options.text: Five pods — the scheduler places pods, never containers directly, so scaling means creating more pods, not adding more containers to one.
options.why: Kubernetes manages pods, not containers directly, so scale-out is expressed entirely in terms of the number of pods, not containers packed into one.

options.text: Five containers inside one pod, since a pod is simply Kubernetes' name for a larger container that can hold several processes.
options.why: A pod is not a bigger container; it is a distinct wrapper, and adding more containers to one pod is a co-location decision, not a scaling one.

options.text: Either interpretation is equally correct, since the scheduler treats containers and pods as interchangeable units of placement That framing erases a real distinction the scheduler depends on: it only ever places pods, never bare containers.
options.why: The scheduler places pods specifically; it has no mechanism for placing individual containers independently of the pod that wraps them.

options.text: Five Deployments, one per instance, since each running copy of the service needs its own separate Deployment object.
options.why: A single Deployment already declares a replica count and manages that many pods from one pod template; five separate Deployments would be redundant.

items.rationale: This is the distinction most often missed: the scheduler places pods, not containers, so a pod's containers can never be split across two nodes, and scaling always means creating more pods, never adding more containers to one pod.

items.stem: A pod holds a main application container and a sidecar container that must share the main container's network so it can inspect traffic on `localhost`. Why does putting both in one pod satisfy that requirement?

options.text: Containers in the same pod share a network namespace, one IP address and one port space, so they reach each other over `localhost` by design.
options.why: Pod-level network sharing is exactly the mechanism that lets two tightly coupled containers talk to each other without any external routing.

options.text: Because Kubernetes automatically creates a Service between any two containers placed in the same pod.
options.why: A Service addresses a set of pods from outside, not two containers within the same pod; pod-internal reachability comes from the shared network namespace itself.

options.text: Because every container in a cluster can already reach every other container over `localhost`, regardless of which pod holds it, extending pod-scoped network sharing to the whole cluster.
options.why: Localhost reachability is scoped to containers sharing the same pod's network namespace; it does not extend cluster-wide between unrelated pods.

options.text: Because both containers were built from the same image, which is what grants them a shared network namespace.
options.why: Network namespace sharing is a property of pod membership, not of whether two containers happen to come from the same image.

items.rationale: Containers in a pod share a network namespace, meaning one IP address and one port space between them, which is exactly why a sidecar that must share the main container's network belongs in the same pod rather than a separate one.

items.stem: A failing pod is replaced automatically. Is the replacement the same pod, repaired, or something else?

options.text: Something else — pods are ephemeral, so a failing one is not repaired but replaced by a new pod with a new name and a new IP address.
options.why: Kubernetes treats pods as disposable rather than long-lived: replacement, not repair, is the mechanism.

options.text: The same pod, repaired in place, since Kubernetes preserves a pod's identity and IP address across any failure it recovers from.
options.why: A pod's replacement is a genuinely new pod with a new identity and IP; pods are not repaired and resumed the way a stopped container can be.

options.text: The same pod, but only its IP address changes while its name and configuration stay identical to before the failure.
options.why: Both the name and the IP address change on replacement; nothing about the failed pod's identity is preserved.

options.text: A different pod entirely, created on the same node the failed one was running on, since replacement never crosses node boundaries That framing invents a node-affinity rule for replacement pods that the scheduler does not apply.
options.why: A replacement pod can be scheduled onto any node with capacity; nothing ties it to the specific node the failed pod happened to run on.

items.rationale: Pods are ephemeral: a failing pod is not repaired but replaced, and the replacement is a new pod with a new name and a new IP address — which is exactly why addressing a pod directly is a bug waiting for the next restart.

items.stem: A bare pod is created directly through the Kubernetes API, with no Deployment involved. What limitation does this carry compared to a pod created by a workload controller?

options.text: Nothing keeps a declared count of it, and nothing recreates it if it fails, since a bare pod has no controller reconciling toward a desired replica count.
options.why: A Deployment is what watches and maintains a pod count; a bare pod exists as a one-off with no such supervision behind it.

options.text: It cannot share a network namespace between its own containers the way a Deployment-created pod can.
options.why: Network namespace sharing between containers is a property of the pod itself, present whether or not a workload controller created it.

options.text: It cannot be scheduled onto a node at all, since only Deployment-created pods are eligible for scheduling That framing invents an eligibility restriction the scheduler does not enforce; it schedules any pod regardless of what created it.
options.why: The scheduler places any pod regardless of how it was created; a bare pod is scheduled the same way a Deployment-created one is.

options.text: It automatically becomes a Deployment after its first restart, adopting a replica count of one.
options.why: A bare pod never converts into a Deployment on its own; without one explicitly created, nothing supervises the pod at all.

items.rationale: Bare pods are rarely created directly — a workload controller such as a Deployment is normally what creates them, because it is the controller that watches and maintains a declared replica count; a bare pod has no such supervision and is not recreated if it fails.

items.stem: Deployment, Kubernetes service, and pod all appear in a change request describing a rolling update. Which statement correctly assigns each object's role?

options.text: The Deployment governs how many pods and which version, the Service governs how callers address them, and the pod is where the containers actually run.
options.why: Each object answers a different question: lifecycle and version, stable addressing, and actual execution.

options.text: The Service governs how many pods and which version, and the Deployment only selects existing pods by label without creating anything, swapping which object owns replica count and which one owns addressing.
options.why: This swaps the two roles: the Deployment creates ReplicaSets and declares the replica count, while the Service selects existing pods and creates nothing.

options.text: The pod governs how many replicas should exist, and the Deployment is merely where the containers physically run.
options.why: A pod knows nothing about how many of itself should exist; replica count is declared on the Deployment, not the pod.

options.text: All three objects are interchangeable names for the same underlying Kubernetes resource, differing only by which command created them.
options.why: They are three distinct object types with distinct APIs and responsibilities, not interchangeable names for one resource.

items.rationale: The Deployment/Service/pod comparison separates lifecycle, addressing, and execution: the Deployment declares how many pods and which version, the Service provides a stable address for whichever pods currently match its selector, and the pod is where the containers actually run.

items.stem: An engineer manually deletes one pod belonging to a Deployment declaring three replicas, expecting the application to run with two instances until the next deploy. What actually happens within seconds?

options.text: A replacement pod appears almost immediately, because the controller continuously compares actual state against the declared replica count and corrects the difference.
options.why: Deleting a pod does not change what was declared; the Deployment's controller notices the shortfall and restores it without anyone asking again.

options.text: The Deployment's replica count silently drops to two, since manual deletion is treated as a deliberate scale-down request.
options.why: Manual pod deletion is not interpreted as a scaling instruction; the declared count on the Deployment is untouched by it.

options.text: Nothing happens until the next scheduled deploy, since the Deployment only reconciles state when a new version is rolled out.
options.why: Reconciliation runs continuously, not only at deploy time; a shortfall against the declared count is corrected immediately, independent of any new rollout.

options.text: The Service in front of the pods creates a replacement directly, since it is responsible for maintaining the pod count behind it That framing assigns the Service a replica-count responsibility that belongs to the Deployment's controller instead.
options.why: A Service selects existing pods and creates nothing; maintaining replica count is the Deployment's job through the ReplicaSet it owns.

items.rationale: Because the controller is continuously comparing actual against desired, deleting one of its pods does not reduce the count — the replica count is now unsatisfied, so a replacement pod appears almost immediately.

items.stem: A Deployment's pod template is changed to reference a new image version. What actually happens to the running pods, mechanically?

options.text: A new ReplicaSet is created and scaled up while the old ReplicaSet is scaled down, replacing pods gradually rather than all at once.
options.why: A Deployment creates a ReplicaSet, and the ReplicaSet creates the pods; changing the template creates a new one rather than editing pods in place.

options.text: Every existing pod is edited in place to reference the new image, with no new ReplicaSet or pod ever created.
options.why: Pods are not edited in place for an image change; a new ReplicaSet is created and its pods gradually replace the old ones.

options.text: All old pods are deleted immediately and simultaneously, and new ones are created only after every old one is gone That framing describes a recreate strategy rather than the gradual rolling behaviour a Deployment uses by default.
options.why: A rolling update scales the new ReplicaSet up while scaling the old one down gradually, not an all-at-once delete-then-create sequence.

options.text: The Service in front of the pods is recreated first, and only then are the pods themselves updated to match.
options.why: A Service selects pods by label and needs no recreation when the Deployment's pod template changes; it keeps routing to whatever currently matches.

items.rationale: Changing the pod template creates a new ReplicaSet, which is scaled up while the old one is scaled down, so pods are replaced gradually rather than all at once; each such change is a revision that can be rolled back.

items.stem: A workload needs a stable per-instance identity and its own dedicated storage that must not be shared across replicas. Is a Deployment the right object for it?

options.text: No, a Deployment assumes interchangeable, essentially stateless pods, and a workload needing stable identity and per-instance storage is not its job.
options.why: The Deployment model treats its pods as freely replaceable copies of each other, which conflicts directly with a requirement for per-instance identity.

options.text: Yes, since a Deployment can be configured to assign a fixed identity to each of its replicas by setting the replica count to a specific value.
options.why: The replica count only controls how many interchangeable pods exist; it grants no per-instance identity or dedicated storage to any of them.

options.text: Yes, because attaching a volume to the Deployment's pod template automatically gives each replica its own separate copy of the data.
options.why: A volume declared on a shared pod template does not automatically partition into separate per-replica copies; interchangeable pods from one template share the same storage definition.

options.text: No, but only because Deployments are limited to stateless container images and cannot reference any image running a database.
options.why: A Deployment places no restriction on what the image contains; the actual mismatch is the model's assumption of interchangeable replicas, not the image type.

items.rationale: A Deployment provides declarative updates for pods and ReplicaSets, but it assumes interchangeable, essentially stateless pods — a workload needing stable identity and per-instance storage needs a different workload object built for that purpose.

items.stem: A frontend calls a backend by directly recording one of its pod IP addresses. After a routine redeploy, the frontend cannot reach the backend at all. What is the fix, and why does it hold up across future redeploys?

options.text: Address the backend through a Kubernetes service instead, since it tracks the current set of matching, ready pods automatically and gives callers one address that never changes.
options.why: A Service exists precisely because pod IPs are ephemeral; addressing through it means a redeploy never breaks the caller.

options.text: Pin the backend's Deployment to always reuse the exact same pod IP address on every redeploy, so recording it once remains valid.
options.why: Pod IPs are assigned fresh on each replacement and are not something a Deployment can pin to a fixed value across redeploys.

options.text: Reduce the backend's replica count to exactly one, since a single-replica Deployment is guaranteed to keep the same pod IP forever, treating replica count as if it controlled address stability.
options.why: Even a single-replica Deployment gets a new pod, and therefore a new IP, every time that pod is replaced; replica count does not stabilise the address.

options.text: Mount a shared volume between the frontend and backend so the address can be read from a file instead of hardcoded.
options.why: A volume solves data persistence, not address stability; nothing about a shared volume tracks which pods are currently ready to serve traffic.

items.rationale: "The frontend cannot reach the backend after a redeploy" is the archetypal scenario caused by addressing pods directly instead of through a Service, which tracks the set of matching, ready pods automatically and gives callers a name that never changes.

items.stem: A service needs to be reachable from the public internet through a provider-managed load balancer. Which Service type fits, as opposed to the cluster-internal default?

options.text: LoadBalancer, which exposes the Service externally through a load balancer, typically provisioned by the cloud provider — unlike ClusterIP, the default that stays internal only.
options.why: LoadBalancer is specifically the type built for external exposure; ClusterIP is deliberately unreachable from outside the cluster.

options.text: ClusterIP, since it is the default type and defaults are always the safest choice for any exposure requirement.
options.why: ClusterIP is explicitly internal-only and cannot be reached from outside the cluster no matter how the application is configured.

options.text: NodePort alone, since exposing a port on each node is functionally identical to a provider-managed load balancer That framing treats a manually exposed node port as equivalent to a managed balancer, ignoring the health checking and traffic distribution the latter provides.
options.why: NodePort exposes a port on each node directly, which is a different mechanism from a provider-managed external load balancer, even though both allow outside traffic in.

options.text: A Deployment with `hostNetwork` enabled, bypassing the Service abstraction entirely for external traffic.
options.why: That setting concerns which network namespace a pod uses, not how external clients discover a stable address; it is not the standard mechanism for external exposure.

items.rationale: ClusterIP exposes the Service inside the cluster only and is the default; NodePort additionally exposes it on a port on each node; LoadBalancer exposes it externally through a load balancer, typically provisioned by the cloud provider.

items.stem: A Service is created with a label selector that matches no currently running pod, due to a typo. What is observed, and what is it not?

options.text: The Service exists and resolves normally but has no endpoints, so connections fail — a label mismatch, not a networking fault.
options.why: Everything about the Service object itself is correctly created; only the set of pods it routes to is empty, which is a labeling problem.

options.text: The Service fails to be created at all, since Kubernetes rejects any selector that does not match at least one existing pod That framing invents a validation rule that Kubernetes does not apply when a Service's selector matches nothing.
options.why: Kubernetes does not validate a selector against currently running pods at creation time; the Service is created regardless and simply has no endpoints.

options.text: The Service automatically falls back to routing traffic to any pod in the namespace when its selector matches nothing.
options.why: There is no such fallback; a Service with no matching pods simply has no endpoints and routes to nothing.

options.text: The underlying Deployment is paused automatically until the Service's selector is corrected to match its pods.
options.why: A Deployment operates independently of any Service in front of it; a selector mismatch on the Service has no effect on the Deployment's own reconciliation.

items.rationale: A Service whose selector matches no pods still exists and still resolves, but has no endpoints, so connections fail — an "everything is created, nothing works" symptom that is a label mismatch, not a networking fault.

items.stem: A Deployment's rolling update replaces every pod behind a Service, one at a time, over several minutes. Do callers using the Service's name notice any interruption from the changeover itself?

options.text: No, because the Service selects by label rather than by address, so it keeps answering as the set of matching pods changes underneath it.
options.why: The linkage is labels alone, which is exactly what lets a rolling update swap every pod underneath a Service without the caller ever needing to know.

options.text: Yes, because the Service must be manually recreated after every pod replacement to pick up the new addresses.
options.why: A Service tracks matching, ready pods automatically through its label selector; it requires no manual recreation as pods are replaced.

options.text: Yes, because the Service knows which Deployment produced its pods and must wait for that Deployment's rollout to finish before routing again.
options.why: A Service neither creates pods nor knows which Deployment produced them; the linkage is labels alone, not an awareness of the owning Deployment.

options.text: No, but only because cluster DNS caches the old pod addresses until the rollout is fully finished.
options.why: Continuity comes from the Service tracking ready pods by label in real time, not from DNS caching stale addresses through the rollout.

items.rationale: The Service's selector matches labels on pods, and the set of matching, ready pods is tracked automatically as pods come and go — the linkage is labels alone, which is exactly what allows a rolling update to swap every pod underneath without the caller noticing.

items.stem: A cluster loses its control plane for ten minutes because of a networking issue. Do applications already running on healthy nodes stop serving traffic?

options.text: No, pods already running on healthy nodes keep serving; what stops is new scheduling, updates, and any other change to cluster state.
options.why: The control plane makes decisions and records state, but running workloads on healthy nodes do not depend on it being reachable every second to keep serving.

options.text: Yes, every pod in the cluster stops immediately, since the control plane is required continuously for any container to keep running That framing extends the control plane's role into keeping already-running pods alive, which is actually the node's own job.
options.why: A running pod's containers keep executing on their node independent of a momentarily unreachable control plane; nothing about their process execution depends on it directly.

options.text: Yes, but only pods managed by a Deployment stop, while bare pods created directly keep running unaffected.
options.why: Whether a pod is managed by a Deployment or created bare has no bearing on whether it keeps running during a control plane outage; both keep serving on their nodes.

options.text: No, but only Services stop resolving names while the pods behind them keep running unaffected.
options.why: Cluster DNS and Service resolution are not what fails during a brief control plane outage in this scenario; the accurate distinction is scheduling and changes stopping while running workloads continue.

items.rationale: Losing the control plane stops new scheduling and new changes, while pods already running on healthy nodes keep serving traffic — a availability distinction the exam likes because it separates decision-making from execution.

items.stem: A candidate must name the control plane component that watches for newly created pods with no assigned node and picks one for them. Which is it?

options.text: `kube-scheduler`, which selects a node for each unscheduled pod based on its declared resource needs and placement constraints.
options.why: Choosing a node for a pod with no assignment is precisely the scheduler's defined responsibility among the four control plane components.

options.text: `kube-apiserver`, which is the front end for the Kubernetes API and therefore also performs node selection for every pod.
options.why: The API server serves the API and is the only component that talks to etcd, but it does not itself choose nodes for pods; that is the scheduler's job.

options.text: etcd, since it stores all cluster data and therefore also decides which node a new pod is assigned to.
options.why: etcd is the consistent key-value store backing cluster data; it stores decisions made elsewhere but does not itself decide node placement.

options.text: `kube-controller-manager`, which runs the controller processes and therefore also handles new-pod scheduling as one of its controllers.
options.why: The controller manager runs reconciliation controllers for existing objects; assigning a node to a newly created, unscheduled pod is the scheduler's separate, dedicated job.

items.rationale: The four control plane components have cleanly separable jobs: the API server serves the API, etcd stores state, `kube-scheduler` chooses nodes for unscheduled pods, and `kube-controller-manager` reconciles state through its controllers.

items.stem: A team decides to back up only their application data volumes, reasoning that cluster configuration can always be reapplied from source control. Which single control plane component still deserves its own backup, and why?

options.text: etcd, because it is the one stateful control plane component, holding the cluster's actual recorded state rather than something rederivable from manifests alone.
options.why: Every other control plane component is effectively stateless and can be replaced; etcd is where the cluster's live state actually lives.

options.text: `kube-scheduler`, because its decisions about where pods were placed cannot be reconstructed from manifests and must be preserved separately That framing treats past scheduling decisions as needing preservation, when the scheduler simply re-decides placement from current cluster state.
options.why: The scheduler makes placement decisions on the fly rather than storing durable state of its own; nothing here needs a dedicated backup.

options.text: `kube-apiserver`, because it caches every API request it has ever served and would lose that history without a backup.
options.why: The API server is a front end that processes requests against etcd; it is not itself a durable store of request history requiring backup.

options.text: `kube-controller-manager`, because its reconciliation loops must resume from an exact saved point rather than simply restarting fresh.
options.why: A controller's reconciliation loop compares current state to desired state on each pass and does not require resuming from a precise saved checkpoint of its own.

items.rationale: etcd is the consistent, highly available key-value store backing all cluster data — the one stateful control plane piece, which makes it the thing to back up; the other three components are effectively replaceable without their own persisted state.

items.stem: A manifest describing three replicas is applied to a cluster twice in a row, with no changes in between. What happens the second time?

options.text: Nothing changes, because the description names an end state rather than steps, and applying it twice is the same as applying it once.
options.why: Declarative configuration is idempotent by design: describing the same desired state again produces no additional effect once that state already holds.

options.text: Three additional replicas are created, since each apply is treated as an imperative instruction to add that many more instances, rather than as a description of the end state to reconcile toward.
options.why: Applying the same manifest again is not interpreted as an additive instruction; the controller compares to the declared count, which is unchanged, and does nothing further.

options.text: The cluster rejects the second apply outright, since a manifest can only be applied successfully one time per object.
options.why: Reapplying an unchanged manifest is a normal, accepted operation; nothing about declarative configuration limits an object to a single apply.

options.text: All existing pods are deleted and recreated from scratch, since every apply resets the object's state before reapplying it.
options.why: Reconciliation only acts on the difference between actual and desired state; with no difference present, nothing is deleted or recreated.

items.rationale: Because the description names an end state rather than a sequence of steps, applying it twice is the same as applying it once — the imperative alternative, a script of create-and-modify commands, is not safe to re-run in the same way.

items.stem: An operator manually scales a workload up with an imperative command, bypassing its stored manifest. Over time, the replica count drifts back to what the manifest declares. Why?

options.text: A controller compares desired against actual on a loop and acts on the difference, so an out-of-band change is treated as drift to correct, not a new desired state.
options.why: The manifest remains the source of truth the controller reconciles toward; a manual change that never updates it is corrected on the next reconciliation pass.

options.text: The manual command silently fails to take effect at all, so nothing was ever actually scaled up in the first place.
options.why: The manual command does take effect immediately; the drift back happens afterward, as reconciliation corrects the difference from the declared state.

options.text: The manifest automatically updates itself to match whatever the imperative command set, which is why the two appear to converge That framing has the file editing itself, when in fact the controller only edits the live cluster object it manages.
options.why: A manifest in version control does not update itself in response to cluster-side changes; convergence happens because the cluster is pulled back toward the unchanged manifest, not the reverse.

options.text: The Service in front of the workload enforces the original replica count independently of any controller.
options.why: A Service has no role in maintaining replica counts; that is the controller's reconciliation loop acting on the Deployment or similar object.

items.rationale: It is the mechanism behind every self-healing claim: a controller compares desired against actual on a loop and acts on the difference, which is the same reason a manually scaled workload drifts back to the declared count — the manifest is the source of truth, not the momentary imperative change.

items.stem: A team keeps their cluster manifests in version control and treats that repository as the source of truth for what should exist. What justifies calling the file, not the running cluster, the source of truth?

options.text: The file names the end state the cluster is continuously driven toward; the running cluster is only wherever reconciliation currently stands relative to it.
options.why: Because the operating model is desired-state-driven, the declared description is what everything else is measured against, not the other way around.

options.text: It is not actually justified, since the live cluster is always more authoritative than any file describing what it should look like.
options.why: The declarative model inverts that intuition deliberately: the file is what the cluster is continuously reconciled toward, making it the authoritative description.

options.text: Because version control automatically applies every commit to the cluster the instant it is pushed, keeping the two permanently identical without any separate deployment step.
options.why: Version control by itself applies nothing; some separate process or pipeline must submit the manifest before the cluster reconciles toward it.

options.text: Because the control plane refuses to accept any change that was not first committed to version control.
options.why: The control plane enforces no such requirement; it accepts any valid submission regardless of whether it originated from version control.

items.rationale: Desired state is stored through the API server, and controllers observe actual state, compare it with desired state, and act to reduce the difference — which is exactly why manifests belong in version control: the file is the source of truth for what the cluster should look like.

items.stem: Which statement correctly places the CNCF relative to the Linux Foundation and to Kubernetes?

options.text: The CNCF is part of the nonprofit Linux Foundation and hosts Kubernetes as one of its graduated projects, providing infrastructure, events, and marketing rather than technical direction.
options.why: This places the CNCF correctly within the Linux Foundation and correctly separates hosting support from governing authority over Kubernetes.

options.text: The CNCF is the parent organisation of the Linux Foundation, and Kubernetes is governed directly by the CNCF as a result That framing inverts the actual relationship: the CNCF is a program of the Linux Foundation, not the other way around.
options.why: The relationship runs the other way — the CNCF is part of the Linux Foundation, not its parent — and Kubernetes is governed by its own Steering Committee regardless.

options.text: The CNCF hosts only the Linux kernel, and Kubernetes is hosted by a separate, unrelated foundation.
options.why: The CNCF's portfolio is the cloud-native ecosystem, Kubernetes included; the Linux kernel is a Linux Foundation project hosted separately from the CNCF's own portfolio.

options.text: The CNCF is a for-profit vendor consortium that owns the trademarks of every project it hosts, Kubernetes included.
options.why: The CNCF is a nonprofit foundation whose mission is making cloud native computing ubiquitous, not a for-profit vendor consortium.

items.rationale: The Cloud Native Computing Foundation is part of the nonprofit Linux Foundation and hosts a large portfolio of vendor-neutral open source projects, Kubernetes among them, sustaining the ecosystem with infrastructure, events, and marketing rather than technical governance.

items.stem: A candidate reads a question naming both an organisation and a project it hosts, and correctly suspects it is testing whether they collapse hosting and governing into one role. What is the safest general answer to that kind of question?

options.text: State the hosting relationship and the separate governing body explicitly, rather than assuming the host also directs the project technically.
options.why: The exam's recurring pattern is exactly this hosting-versus-governing split, so answering it by naming both roles separately is the reliable strategy.

options.text: Assume the named organisation both hosts and governs, since a foundation prominent enough to host a project usually also directs it That framing conflates hosting infrastructure with technical direction, which CNCF projects deliberately keep separate.
options.why: This is exactly the collapsing of roles the question is designed to catch; hosting foundations in this exam consistently do not govern the projects they host.

options.text: Assume the project governs itself entirely with no relationship to any hosting organisation at all.
options.why: The hosting relationship is real and examinable — funding, infrastructure, and marketing support genuinely come from the host — so denying it entirely is also wrong.

options.text: Treat the question as unanswerable without knowing the specific committee names involved.
options.why: The exam expects the vocabulary and the shape of the relationship, not memorised committee membership; specific names are not required to answer correctly.

items.rationale: This is the same shape as the Linux Foundation's relationship to the Linux kernel, and a question that names one organisation and one project is usually probing whether the candidate collapses the two roles into one — naming hosting and governing as distinct answers it correctly.

items.stem: A new open source project applies to join the CNCF's portfolio. What does progressing from sandbox to graduated status actually represent?

options.text: Demonstrated adoption and governance maturity, tracked by the CNCF as hosting stages, not a transfer of technical direction to the foundation.
options.why: Graduation reflects how mature and adopted a project has become under CNCF hosting criteria; it says nothing about who directs the project technically.

options.text: The point at which the CNCF takes over day-to-day technical decisions from the project's own maintainers.
options.why: Day-to-day technical authority stays with each project's own maintainers and governance structures regardless of hosting stage.

options.text: A rebranding step in which the project's name and trademark transfer fully to Linux Foundation ownership.
options.why: Graduation is a hosting-maturity classification, not a trademark or naming transfer event of that kind.

options.text: The moment a project is required to switch its container runtime to containerd as a condition of remaining hosted That framing invents a runtime requirement the CNCF does not attach to any hosting stage.
options.why: Hosting stage has no bearing on which container runtime a project uses; the CNCF imposes no such technical requirement as a condition of graduation.

items.rationale: Projects enter at sandbox level and progress through incubating to graduated as adoption and governance maturity are demonstrated; a Technical Oversight Committee maintains the foundation's technical vision, while day-to-day technical authority stays with each project's own maintainers.
